en: The *Adhyātmasāraśataka* composed by the Great Paṇḍita Śrīprabhākaragupta (with commentary). Om, homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!

Since the establishment of any entity whatsoever is not found anywhere through the various means of accomplishment (*siddhicāra*) that bring about the bliss of the cessation of unity and plurality regarding earth and the other elements;
All this, up to consciousness itself, is here entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; it does not manifest from nowhere, but rather according to the constraints of place, time, and form. (1)

Having bowed perpetually to the Goddess Ugratārā, who bestows incomparable bliss; to the Sugata and his Saṅgha, together with the Dharma, throughout the duration of cyclic existence; and likewise to my Guru, whose lotus feet are ever-present—I shall today explain, in brief and in accordance with the desire of my disciples, the meaning of the *Adhyātmasāra*, which possesses a multitude of excellent qualities.
Just as was the desire of his kinsmen for the adornment of their hearts and their fame,
so did Śiromaṇi speak with him according to his ability regarding that matter.
It neither meets nor dissolves; what? The establishment of the entity (vastusiddhi). Of what? Of those [elements], earth and so forth.
How? Somewhere, anywhere, from somewhere; that is, from wherever.
By whom? By the spies of the Siddhas—that is, by those who investigate the Siddhas.
Of what nature were they? They were manifold.
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
They were characterized by the bliss of the cessation of both the one and the many.
It exists.
What? All of that.
In what state?
Up to consciousness.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the absence of intrinsic nature.
Why? Because it does not throb—that is, it does not manifest—everywhere, on all sides. What is it that does not manifest? That entire range ending with consciousness.
Of what? Of place, time, and form.
Why? Because it would be causeless (*akasmāt*).
For what reason? Because of the restriction (*niyamāt*).
Where? In this saṃsāra. || 1 ||

Therefore, I bow to that one who is reached through yoga— the cause of the birth of all worlds, distinct from earth, water, fire, air, ether, and consciousness; whether he be the omnipresent Lord as conceived by some, or emptiness, or otherwise, he is that upon whose refuge all sovereignty depends.
He sits; he exists.
Who? Someone.
Of what nature?
The cause is the reason. Of what? Of origination, that is, arising. Of what things? Of all worlds.
Why? Because of that.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
The blue [mountain] of the earth...
That which is distinct from fire, wind, space, and consciousness—who is that? It is this Lord (Īśa).
Of what nature is he?
He is all-pervading and sovereign.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is beloved and esteemed.
Which? Emptiness. Of what nature?
It exists as the Lord.
How? Either in this way or otherwise. To whom? To him (the Buddha). What do I do? I bow; I pay homage. Who am I? I.
Whom? That all-pervading Lord.
Of what nature?
Attainable through yoga, that is, reached by means of meditative absorption (samādhi).
What comes to be?
Sovereignty over all?
Why?
Because of following that. || 2 ||
Because they do not realize this, these scholars, their hearts defiled, engage in dispute by imagining various doctrines;

thus being mocked, failing to attain the state of the Self, blinded by delusion and destroyed by death, they wander through this saṃsāra from the auspicious to the inauspicious until the end of existence. (3)
They wander and roam about; who? These scholars. Where? In this saṃsāra.
How? Until the end of existence, from birth.
Why? Because of the unwholesome and the wholesome.
Having done what? Without having attained, without having fully reached.
In this manner, by such a way;
[they attain] the state of the well-recited path, which is the path to liberation.
Of what nature are these wise ones?
Blinded by delusion and blinded by ignorance;
furthermore, how are they characterized?
They are being mocked and ridiculed.
Being of what nature? Engaging in.
What? Dispute, that is, deliberation.
Having done what? Having conceptualized, that is, having reflected.
What? A manifold view, that is, a diverse opinion.
Why? Due to lack of understanding, that is, non-familiarity. Of what? Of that right knowledge.
Of what nature are they? They have turbid hearts, meaning their minds are possessed of conceptual constructions. Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They are destroyed by death; they are seized by death. || 3 ||
In the Buddhist, Sāṃkhya, Jain, Vaiṣṇava, and Śaiva traditions, the existence of rebirth is accepted through both the path of reasoning and scripture.
If the Cārvāka does not accept this, what is lost by one person alone? For the lack of experience on the part of those born blind does not negate the existence of the moon.
It exists.
What? The existence of birth, which is the grasping of birth. Of what nature is it?
That which is desired and longed for.
How? Furthermore, by whom?
By means of both reasoning and scripture— that is, by means of both logic and authoritative tradition—
in what? In the Buddhist [system],
and not only in the Buddhist, but also in the Sāṃkhya.
Not only in Sāṃkhya and in the doctrine of the Kṣapaṇakas; not only in the doctrine of the Kṣapaṇakas and in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition];
and not only in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition] and on the Śaiva path.
He does not conceive, he does not think.
Who? The Cārvāka nihilist. What is that? The existence of birth.
And how [could it be] if it existed? Who [would say so]? The Cārvāka.
Of what nature is he? Solitary.
How? But how could it be? How? What would happen?
By whom? By a single Cārvāka.
It does not exist. What is this non-existence? It is miserliness. Of what? Of that which possesses the moon—that is, of one for whom the moon exists.
For how, indeed, could it be for one who is of what nature?
Not for one who does not experience, who does not perceive. Of whom? Of those born blind, of those whose blindness is innate. || 4 ||
The elements themselves are not established as non-empty by the force of valid cognition, because the nature of being a real entity cannot be proven due to the absence of both unity and plurality.

Since this very nature of entities—such as the composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth—which was proposed [by others], is obscured from afar, how then can there be a doctrine of elemental consciousness (*bhūtacaitanyavāda*) here? || 5 ||
They neither succeed nor fail; they do not come into being.
What are they? The elements, such as earth and the rest.
Of what nature are they?
Non-empty things are not established; rather, empty things are established.
Why? By the force of valid cognition—that is, by the power of the means of knowledge. How is this not certain?
What? That which.
Of what nature?
The establishment of the reality of the thing.
Why? Because of the departure of unity and plurality—that is, because of the absence of oneness and manifoldness.
How so? Because (yat), for which reason, it exists (asti).
What is this?
Of what nature is it?
It is that which has been commenced and undertaken.
What? Therein, of what nature is it? It is the essential nature of entities such as the whole (avayavin) and so forth. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Obscured from afar, lost from afar.
What? The doctrine of objective consciousness (*bhūtacaitanyavāda*) and the doctrine of instrumental consciousness (*pramāṇacaitanyavāda*).
Why? Where? [It is not found anywhere.]
In this saṃsāra. || 5 ||

Although the multitude of elements accepted by various philosophical systems remains at all times within the range of everyone’s experience, one should not accept that which, despite being experienced and accepted, is unreal; for does the sky not appear to every living being here as if it were bent downward?
There exists a totality (samaṣṭi).
What is it? It is the aggregate of elements, the collection beginning with earth.
Of what nature is it?
"Accepted" means agreed upon. In what? In the manifold doctrine (*bahuvidhamate*). How? "In whatever way," that is, if it proceeds or functions in any manner whatsoever.
What? A multitude of beings.
Of what nature?
Situated in experience, that is, being perceived.
Of whom? Of all beings, beginning with humans. How? At all times, always.
In no way whatsoever is it certain.
What? Unreality, which is falsity.
Of what nature? That which is to be grasped.
Of what?
Of acceptance, that is, of approval.
From what? From the experience of which, that is, from the cognition of which.
Why? Because it is not investigated.
It does not appear; it does not manifest.
What? Space.
Of what nature? Bent down, that is, bowed. Of whom? Of every living being, of every creature.
Where? In this saṃsāra. How? What? || 6 ||
Furthermore, as long as the cognition of one thing does not cease until that of another arises, it cannot enter the path of linguistic usage in an unmixed state;

and since that cessation of one occurs simultaneously with the cognition of another, if one were to accept this [view], then a knower of a single thing would become an omniscient knower of everything. (7)
It would not exist; it would not come to be.
What? The thought of cessation, the thought of investigation.
Of what? Of another, of something else.
How? Furthermore, moreover; where? Elsewhere;
how far? Until he goes, until he departs.
What? Something. What kind of thing? The path of worldly activity, the course of conventional practice.
Of what nature is it?
Unmixed;
exceedingly minute.
How, then, and in what manner does it come to be?
What is that cessation? It is the state of non-existence.
Of what? Of anything else.
Where? In this saṃsāra.
And how? Of what?
Of which awakening, or of another?
From where? From all sides, everywhere.
It would be; it exists. Who? Someone:
a single knower in non-dual knowledge.

Furthermore, what is he like? He is the knower of all aspects (sarvākārajña), the omniscient one regarding everything. Under what condition? When that [omniscience] is accepted, when it is agreed upon. || 7 ||
If the non-existence of the perceptible here is the indicator by itself, it is not so; for non-existence cannot be unrelated, since negation is never known anywhere without a basis.

Because difference is established through recourse to mutual dependence, and because of the absence [of such dependence], all this worldly discourse—which ends in delusion—is therefore just like a dream. (8)
It does not exist. What? Non-existence. Of what nature?
It is absolute and non-dual.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the absence of the visible, which is the absence of any existing object.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "cognizable" (gamaka), meaning it is within the range of sensory perception.
Where? In this world of saṃsāra.
How so? That which does not occur. What is it? A negation, a refutation. Of what nature is it?
"Nihsambandhaḥ" means devoid of connection.
Of what nature is he?
He is "viditaḥ," meaning known.
Somewhere, anywhere.
Why? Because.
How indeed does it exist? What is it?
This is "vyavahṛti," which means worldly transaction or conventional practice. Of what nature is it? It is "all" (sarvā). Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Delusion is confusion;
furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is just like a dream, resembling a dream.
Why? For that reason. How is it determined thus?
Why? Because of separation—that is, because of distinction.
Of what? Of the establishment of difference, that is, the establishment of specific distinction.
Why? Because it has recourse to mutual dependence, that is, because it follows upon a circular dependency. || 8 ||
Just as here, despite the absence of any real entity, coming and going and so forth exist—being like an illusion or a dream due to delusion—so too does another birth exist.
Having cast aside doubt arising from the words of those fallen into false views, the wise should effect the destruction of birth through the method of practicing yoga. (9)
It exists.
What? Coming and going, such as departure and arrival.
Where? In this world of saṃsāra.
In what? In the absence of an object, in the absence of a substance.
How? In whatever way.
Why? From delusion, under the influence of ignorance.
It exists;
what is it? It is the other.
What is the other? Birth.
And how, and of what nature? Like an illusion and a dream; that is, similar to an illusion and a dream. How? Just so, exactly as it is.
Why? Because of the words of those fallen into false views, following the doctrine of nihilists (*nāstika*).
What is to be enjoined, ordained, or performed? The destruction of birth—that is, the cessation of arising. Having done what?
Having cast aside and avoided;
by whom? By the wise, the learned;
by what means? By the method of practicing yoga.
What? Doubt, the state of uncertainty.
From what? From the words of one fallen into false views.
And how? In some way or other. || 9 ||
Just as there is a clear experience of distinction among people even within the entire world of delusion due to the conjunction of the diversity of karma,

so too, through the practice of yoga, a specific excellence is achieved by means of perceiving the marks of the multitude of vast virtues, which results in the attainment of the abandonment of the fear of worldly existence.
There exists a totality (samaṣṭi).
What is it? Experience, that is, the act of experiencing.
Of whom? Of people, that is, of the worlds.
Of what? Of "vaiśiṣṭya," that is, of a distinction (*viśeṣa*). Like what? Like what (*yadvat*).
How? Clearly (*sphuṭam*).
Why? Because of the connection with the variety of karma, that is, the connection with the various [results] of the auspicious and inauspicious.
By what? By falsehood (mithyātva).
Of whom?
For all the worlds—that is, for all transmigrating beings—it is somehow determined that it shall be accomplished; indeed, it is accomplished. What is it? It is the distinction, the difference.

Of what? Of the accomplishment of abandoning the fear of existence (*bhava*), that is, of the success described as resulting from the removal of the dread of *saṃsāra*. From what? From the practice of yoga, that is, from the means of achieving yoga.
By what? By the observation of the signs of the multitude of vast qualities, that is, by the beholding of the marks of the collection of great virtues.
Like what? Like that; in exactly that same way.
Howsoever. || 10 ||

First, there is mastery over the body through the attainment of a divine body; thereafter, mastery over speech arises from the power of words, as one becomes a speaker [of truth] through the perfection of speech.

Mastery over the mind comes from bringing the senses under one's own control, whereby the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are easily brought under subjection by oneself; thus is the supreme accomplishment attained. (11)
Is there anything? This is sovereignty over the body, which is bodily autonomy.
Why? First, at the outset. From what? From attainment, from acquisition. Of what?
Of the body—that is, of the divine body. Does it exist? Yes. What is it? The capacity for speech, because its perfection has been described.
Of what nature is it?
It is not merely recounted, but rather spoken.
What is that? What is it?
Mastery over speech. Of what? Of the accomplishment of speech, that is, the accomplishment of utterance.
It exists.
What? Sovereignty over the mind, mastery of the mind.
Why? Because of bringing [the senses] under one's own control, because of making them subject to oneself.
Of what? Of the sense organs, such as the eye and so forth.
By what? By happiness.
What comes to be? Supreme accomplishment.
By what? By the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the others. Of what nature?
Being produced by one's own power, they are "well-arisen" (*sadbhiḥ*), meaning they have arisen independently.
How? "In this way" (*ittham*), by means of this manner.
How so? || 11 ||

Due to the absence of practice in the cultivation of yoga, one possesses a coarse view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), is afflicted, falls under the power of all manner of calamities, and gradually suffers the loss of life.
Upon the abandonment of the body, with the mind still bound by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one is born again like a dream; thus one proceeds once more in this same way, and so on endlessly. (12)
It exists.
What is it? The world. Of what nature is it? It possesses the coarse view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Why?
Due to the absence of the practice of yoga,
who becomes [what]? The yogi.
Subject to every misfortune, he has encountered endless suffering.
Of what nature is he?
He is afflicted, meaning possessed by disease.
It occurs.
What? The loss of the vital breaths. By what?
Gradually, step by step.
It would be; it exists.
What? The world. Of what nature? One whose mind is bound by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Why? Because of the abandonment of the body, that is, the destruction of the body.
How? Once again.
He goes, he departs.
What world?
Which one? That which is beginningless and endless, and whose births are infinite.
How? Again and again.
Thus, in this manner. || 12 ||
Since, here in this world, the extent of the limbs of the sun and moon outside the circles of the winds is fifteen with a quarter;
and from the transition multiplied by five and sixty, there is a severance of one and a quarter channels per day, occurring in a sequence of two.
It occurs.
What? The expansion of its own limbs.
Of which two? Of the sun and the moon, the sun and the moon.
Why? Because of their flow, because of their movement. Of what? Of the spheres, that is, the spheres of wind. Where? Here, in this body.
Of what nature is the expansion of his own limbs?
It is both entirely outside and entirely inside; why?
For the following reason.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is "rudrasaṃkhya," numbering eleven.
Of what nature is he?
With one quarter added, it becomes one;
what is it? That expansion of its own limbs.
Of what nature is it?
It is "with a quarter," meaning accompanied by a fourth part.
Why? Because of the transition multiplied by the arrows—that is, due to the transference multiplied by five.
Why? Because there are fifty-six—that is, fifty-six more [than fifty]. What is it that occurs? That severance of the channels, the destruction of the *nāḍikās*.
By what? By the sequence of the number two, that is, by the order of counting as twos. How? Daily, every day. From where? From this [point], from the solar transit (saṃkrānti). || 13 ||
In this world, the entire seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) are seized by time; because there is no departure from that [seizure], it lasts for a hundred years.

Therefore, in the Vedas and other scriptures, this person is described as having a lifespan of a hundred years, being distinct for all beings—whether asuras, gods, or mortals—according to their respective months.
It becomes what? A thousand. Of what? Of the channels (nāḍikānām), that is, of the veins (nāḍīnām).
How much? It is called the seventy-two-fold.
Where? In this body.
Of what nature is it?
The whole is the collective totality.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It would be seized by time, that is, seized by death.
Who? That person.
Of what nature?
Described, that is, uttered.
Why? From a hundred years—that is, from a century.
In what? In the Śruti and so forth, meaning the Vedas and so forth.
And how? By what means?
For that reason.
Why? Because by its removal, there is no destruction of the channels.
Of what nature is the person?

"Śatāyuḥ" means having a lifespan of a hundred years. By what means? By their respective years inherent within themselves. Being of what nature? [The answer follows: Being one who has reached the state of a hundred years.
He is distinct from asuras, suras, mortals, and so forth; He is distinct from daityas, gods, humans, and so forth. Furthermore, of what nature is He? He is the All-inclusive (Samasta). || 14 ||

Just as the sun, having reached its full maturity, traverses the entire zodiac circle in due order—neither bypassing the moon nor the lunar day—as time revolves through every mansion; so too, within the body, the sun and the moon, along with the wheel of the vital winds (vātacakra), move in the same manner. 15.
It does not exist.
Which [does not exist]? The *taraṇi*, the sun.
Of what nature is it?
"Prāuḍhaḥ" means capable.
To do what?
To eat, that is, to consume or devour.
Is it not the constellation Ṛkṣa that is the Kṣatra? It is not merely Ṛkṣa, nor is it merely the Moon (Candra),
nor is it merely the Moon or the lunar day (Tithi).
Of what nature?
Entire, that is, collective.
How? Certainly, thus.
By what? By the sequence of the carriage, that is, by the order of their movement. From where? Everywhere in the zodiacal sign (rāśi).
Like what? Just as [in the previous case].
It revolves and moves.
What? Time, namely Rāhu. What is it?
This zodiacal circle.
Of what nature is it?
It is entirely without remainder.
How? That [arises] from that.
By what? By way of sequence, that is, in due order.
In what? In the body, that is, the physical frame.
How? Generally, that is, for the most part.
How? In that very same way. And what happens? What? Time, Rāhu.
Of what nature is he?
Mature and capable.
To do what? To eat, that is, to consume.
Who? The sun and the moon. Not only the sun and the moon, but also the wind-wheel, that is, the collection of winds. || 15 ||
Even when the body is nourished, the power that is extremely harsh in youth reaches the inner channel and, having gone upward, takes the moon to the crown of the head;
from the *vajra* it leads it outside, and then returns to the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra. Due to the destruction of the channels, one who possesses wrinkles and grey hair proceeds to the *Kālacakra*.
It leads, that is, it causes to reach. What? Power. Whom? The moon, which is the bodhicitta.
What? The external, that which is outside.
From what? From the vajra, the thunderbolt.
And it approaches, and it comes.
What? The crown-cakra, the stainless cakra.
Having done what? Having taken up, having grasped. Where? On the head, at the top of the skull.
Furthermore, having done what? Having attained. What? The internal channel (antarnāḍī), that is, the inner tube. Being of what nature?
Being fully encompassed, being completely attained;
where? Above, on the upper side; of what nature?
Excessively harsh and exceedingly sharp in its brilliance—in what? In youth, in the prime of life. Under what conditions? When the body is flourishing and the moon is full.
And furthermore, somehow or other it proceeds—that is, it goes forth.
Who? A living being.
What? The mouth of the wheel of time.
In what state? Being possessed of wrinkles and grey hair, with shriveled skin and withered locks.
Why? Due to the destruction of the channels (nāḍīs), that is, from the complete drying up of the vessels. || 16 ||
Having abandoned even the pleasure born of passion during lunar and solar eclipses, this Caṇḍālī secretly and incessantly melts the lunar element;
since [this occurs] even for one who has practiced lifelong celibacy from childhood, embodied beings whose bodies are agitated by power are subject to time.
It should cause to melt, it should cause to flow.
What? This central Caṇḍālī.
What? The lunar element.
How? Constantly and without interruption.
Again, how?
Silently and without sound.
Having done what? Having abandoned, that is, having relinquished.
What? Happiness. Of what nature?
Born of love, arising from love;
how indeed was it determined?
Furthermore, of what nature was it?
There would be, or it might be, an eclipse of the moon and sun—the time of the swallowing of the moon and sun.
What? Old age and so forth, up to Buddhahood and so forth.
Where? Here, in this body. How far? Up to what point? Why? From childhood celibacy—that is, from the practice of celibacy beginning below the age of sixteen.
In some way or another,
embodied beings— what kind of beings?—
come into existence; they are subject to time, that is, under the power of death.
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
Their bodies were overwhelmed by power, meaning their frames were rendered incapacitated. Why? Because of that state of decay. ||17||17||
